topic.subject: social
topic.title: Water resources
topic.scope: water scarcity, multipurpose river projects and dams, debates over dams, rainwater harvesting, traditional systems

nodes.name: Scarcity is not just low rainfall

misconceptions.statement: Water scarcity is caused only by lack of rainfall.
misconceptions.why: Students equate scarcity with drought, ignoring human consumption patterns.
misconceptions.fix: Scarcity can occur even with sufficient rainfall due to over-exploitation, pollution, and unequal distribution.

probe.question: Can a region with high rainfall face water scarcity?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because rain provides enough water for everyone.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Dams are always the best solution to prevent floods.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that if a structure is built to hold water, it must prevent all flooding.
misconceptions.fix: Dams often worsen floods during heavy releases or due to sedimentation, and they disrupt natural river flow.

probe.question: Do dams always stop floods?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, they hold back all the extra water.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Rainwater harvesting is only for rural areas.
misconceptions.why: Students associate traditional systems with villages and ignore modern urban applications.
misconceptions.fix: Rainwater harvesting is highly effective in urban areas through rooftop collection to recharge groundwater.

probe.question: Can cities use rainwater harvesting?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a traditional village practice.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Water scarcity happens only in deserts and dry regions, never in places with big rivers.
misconceptions.why: Students link scarcity with visible dryness and ignore the problem of uneven availability and demand.
misconceptions.fix: Scarcity can occur even in areas with plenty of water, because of overuse, pollution and unequal access, as in Indian cities on large rivers.

probe.question: Can a city located beside a large river face a water shortage? Why or why not?
probe.wrong_answer: No, a city next to a big river always has enough water.

misconceptions.statement: Industrial pollution of water does not cause water scarcity because the water is still there.
misconceptions.why: Students equate scarcity with the quantity of water and ignore quality.
misconceptions.fix: Polluted water is unfit for use, so it reduces the usable supply; NCERT lists pollution from industries and agriculture as a cause of scarcity.

probe.question: A river has plenty of water but is badly polluted by factories. Is there a water scarcity for people using it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, as long as the river has a lot of water there is no scarcity.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only the quantity of water matters, not quality

misconceptions.statement: Population growth affects only the food supply, not the availability of water.
misconceptions.why: Students link population with food and housing but not with per-person water use.
misconceptions.fix: More people need more water for domestic use, irrigation and industry, so per capita availability falls and over-exploitation of water rises.

probe.question: How does a growing population affect water resources?
probe.wrong_answer: It only increases the demand for food and has no effect on water availability.

misconceptions.root_belief: Population pressure does not involve water demand

misconceptions.statement: Irrigation and green revolution farming use very little water compared with households.
misconceptions.why: Students see daily household use but not the large water needs of crops and farms.
misconceptions.fix: Agriculture, especially irrigated crops like rice, wheat and sugarcane, is the biggest user of water and has led to falling groundwater levels.

probe.question: Which group uses the largest share of water: households or irrigated agriculture?
probe.wrong_answer: Households, because people use water every day and farms use only a little.

misconceptions.root_belief: Visible daily use equals the largest water use

misconceptions.statement: Nehru called dams the temples of modern India because they are religious places built on rivers.
misconceptions.why: Students take the word temple literally and confuse the metaphor with worship.
misconceptions.fix: Nehru used 'temples of modern India' because dams bring industrial development, agricultural growth and jobs, not because they are religious.

probe.question: Why did Jawaharlal Nehru call dams the 'temples of modern India'?
probe.wrong_answer: Because temples were built near dams and people worship there.

misconceptions.root_belief: Metaphors in textbooks are literal statements

misconceptions.statement: A multipurpose river project is built only to produce electricity.
misconceptions.why: Students identify dams such as Bhakra Nangal with hydroelectric power alone.
misconceptions.fix: Multipurpose projects serve several aims at once: irrigation, hydroelectricity, water supply, flood control, inland navigation and fish breeding.

probe.question: Why are dams like Hirakud called multipurpose projects?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they are used to generate electricity only.

misconceptions.root_belief: Dams exist for a single purpose

misconceptions.statement: Dams have only benefits and cause no harm to rivers or the environment.
misconceptions.why: Textbook praise of development leads students to ignore ecological costs.
misconceptions.fix: Dams disturb the natural flow of rivers, cause sedimentation, harm aquatic life and vegetation, and can increase flood risk and conflicts, leading to protests like Narmada Bachao Andolan.

probe.question: Why did people protest against the Sardar Sarovar dam?
probe.wrong_answer: They had no real reason, as dams cause no damage to the environment.

misconceptions.root_belief: Development projects have no negative effects

misconceptions.statement: People displaced by dams are always fully compensated and resettled, so they lose nothing.
misconceptions.why: Students assume government projects automatically give fair rehabilitation.
misconceptions.fix: Many displaced people, often tribals and the poor, lost land and livelihoods and were not adequately rehabilitated, which fuelled movements like Narmada Bachao Andolan.

probe.question: Why did displaced people oppose dams like Sardar Sarovar?
probe.wrong_answer: They did not oppose it because they were all given good land and homes.

misconceptions.root_belief: Official projects always treat affected people fairly

misconceptions.statement: Traditional water harvesting methods like tankas and johads are outdated and useless today.
misconceptions.why: Students think modern technology like dams has replaced old methods.
misconceptions.fix: Tankas, johads, kuls and bamboo drip irrigation are low-cost, local and still used; Gendathur in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu's compulsory roof-top harvesting show their value.

probe.question: Are traditional methods like johads and tankas useful for water conservation today?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are old and only modern dams can conserve water.

misconceptions.root_belief: Old methods are always inferior to modern ones
